tour.title: CLI Orientation
tour.description: Start with the product-facing CLI contract alongside the application entry wiring, since this repository has no README and the generated errgen main is not the primary product path. The spec explains the user-visible command surface, while main.go and root.go show how tuck starts, handles metadata shortcuts, registers subcommands, and applies consistent command error behavior. This gives you both the purpose of the project and the runtime doorway into the rest of the code.
tour.languageLesson: Go command-line applications often keep the executable entry thin and place reusable application wiring in internal packages; this keeps startup behavior testable without exposing private implementation packages outside the module.

tour.title: Command Tree
tour.description: Building on the root command, these files divide the CLI into source, package, and file command families. They translate the specification from Step 1 into urfave/cli command definitions, arguments, and action callbacks. Reading them together shows the main vertical slices users interact with before the code hands work to command adapters and domain logic.

tour.title: Command Adapters
tour.description: The command adapter layer is where parsed CLI requests become structured operations and output payloads. Source commands manage configured source registries, package commands discover or use package contents, and file commands adopt or inspect individual managed files. This step bridges the user-facing command tree from Step 2 to the core domain, planning, and status packages that follow.

tour.title: Input and Rendering
tour.description: Before following business logic deeper, understand the boundary code that standardizes arguments, flags, output formats, and error records. The analysis ranks renderer.go as the highest fan-in production node, so many command paths rely on this rendering contract being stable. Together these files explain how tuck keeps human output, JSON envelopes, color policy, hints, and exit behavior consistent across commands.

tour.title: Domain and Manifest
tour.description: Now move into the vocabulary the command adapters depend on: active sources, target scopes, logical-to-physical path mapping, and source manifests. The manifest milestone spec documents the intended .tuck.toml behavior, while the code loads, validates, initializes, marshals, and writes that contract. This layer turns CLI verbs into a concrete model of the source tree tuck operates on.
tour.languageLesson: Go's internal/ directory is an import boundary: packages under internal can be imported only by code inside the parent tree, which reinforces tuck's private layered architecture.

tour.title: Source Registry State
tour.description: Tuck separates repository manifests from machine-local state about configured source roots, defaults, and persistence paths. The state package has several high fan-in files in the topology results, signaling that validation, deterministic marshaling, and path selection are foundational contracts. Read this after the domain layer to see how tuck remembers the sources that later package and planning operations consume.
tour.languageLesson: TOML works well for small human-readable state files, but deterministic marshaling is important so tests and users can distinguish meaningful state changes from formatting noise.

tour.title: Package Discovery
tour.description: With sources and manifests available, the packages layer discovers package contents and resolves package references from configured source trees. The fan-out ranking identifies packages.go as one of the broadest production files, making it a useful overview of how source state expands into package trees. resolve.go complements it by choosing the active enabled source before discovery and planning begin.

tour.title: Planning Operations
tour.description: The plan layer converts selected sources, package references, and file requests into concrete filesystem mutation plans. operation.go is a high fan-out orchestrator for source selection, package resolution, privilege handling, and apply behavior, while use, adopt, eject, and apply implement the main write paths. This is where the command adapters from Step 3 become safe, inspectable changes on disk.

tour.title: Status Evaluation
tour.description: Status operations reuse the same source, package, and path concepts but classify what already exists instead of planning new mutations. status.go and scope.go resolve the active context, classify targets, and translate those classifications into file or package status entries. The shared status output adapter then makes those results available to both human and JSON renderers.

tour.title: Shared Utilities
tour.description: Several cross-cutting helpers support the domain, planning, state, and status layers without owning a user workflow themselves. Path utilities centralize normalization, containment, target translation, and symlink payload behavior, while apperr provides the shared error wrapper vocabulary. Understanding this layer explains why higher-level packages can focus on decisions instead of reimplementing path and error mechanics.

tour.title: Error Generation
tour.description: The errgen command is a developer tool rather than the main tuck product entry point, but it explains how typed package error helpers are produced across internal packages. The generator implementation and generated apperr files connect back to the shared error behavior used by command output in Step 4. The mise configuration shows how generation fits into the repository's repeatable check workflow.
tour.languageLesson: Code generation is common in Go projects when repeated boilerplate must stay consistent; the generated files should be treated as build artifacts derived from a smaller source of truth.

tour.title: Acceptance Testing
tour.description: After the architecture is clear, read the testing strategy and acceptance harness to see how tuck verifies complete CLI behavior. The harness creates controlled HOME, state, config, and source fixture environments, while txtar scripts describe user-level scenarios for foundation and package workflows. This capstone ties the command surface from Step 1 to end-to-end behavior that protects future changes.
tour.languageLesson: Txtar fixtures bundle scripts and virtual files into one readable test artifact, which makes CLI acceptance tests easy to review as executable documentation.

tour.title: Project Configuration
tour.description: Finish with the configuration files that make the repository reproducible for contributors and tools. go.mod and go.sum define the Go module and dependency checksums, .codebook.toml tunes spelling checks, and the backlog documents the remaining product roadmap. These files are not runtime code, but they explain how the project is built, reviewed, and evolved.
